title: The Last Programming Language Won’t Be for Humans
text: Coding agents already write close to half of professional developers’ code, yet trust in that code is falling. This post maps six futures for programming, the evidence behind each, and the four gates between today and a language only machines read. My bet: people keep writing precise specifications, and everything beneath them stops being written for human eyes.

title: The Last Programming Language Won’t Be for Humans
text:
1. Coding has died before
In 1957, John Backus’s team released Fortran as an “automatic coding system” (Backus et al. 1957). The compiler would write the machine code, and much of the programmer’s job was supposed to go with it. In 2023, Andrej Karpathy declared English “the hottest new programming language” (Karpathy 2023). Two years later he named “vibe coding”: building software by talking to a model and never reading the code it writes (Karpathy 2025).
In between, Edsger Dijkstra made the case for the defence. Programming in natural language, he argued in 1978, is foolish, because precision needs formal notation (Dijkstra 1978).
Both sides were half right. The layer being mourned never died; it sank. Nobody writes machine code by hand anymore, yet every program still becomes machine code. I think the same thing is happening again, one level up. Typing code is dying; code is not. What humans write is moving up, toward the specification. What machines exchange is sinking below readability: first into something no human needs to read, and eventually into something no human can.
Making that case takes three things: an honest look at where we are, a map of where today’s research leads, and an account of the gates between the two.

title: The Last Programming Language Won’t Be for Humans
text:
2. What the data says
Two claims circulate more than any others: that coding is dead, and that almost nobody writes code by hand anymore. Neither survives the surveys.
JetBrains asked more than 15,000 professional developers how last month’s code was produced. On average, they said agents had written about 47% of it on their own, while 27% was still written entirely by hand (JetBrains Research 2026). Over half now hand-write less than a fifth of their code, and one in five writes none at all. But the fully agentic group, where agents produce more than 80% of the code, is still a 22% minority. Ninety percent of professional developers use a coding agent at work at least weekly (Bogdanov 2026). At the top end, Google says 75% of its new code is AI-generated and approved by engineers, up from 25% in 2024 (Semafor 2026).
Adoption, then, is solved. Trust is not. Stack Overflow’s survey of 49,000 developers found that 84% use or plan to use AI tools, but only 29% trust their output, down from 40% the year before. Another 46% actively distrust it, and 45% say debugging AI-generated code takes longer than writing it themselves (Stack Overflow 2025). Sonar found that 96% of developers do not fully trust AI code to be correct, yet only 48% always check it before committing (Sonar 2026).
The productivity evidence is just as mixed. In METR’s 2025 randomized controlled trial, experienced open-source developers working in their own repositories were 19% slower with AI, while believing it had sped them up by about 20% (Becker et al. 2025). An earlier Copilot trial found a 56% speed-up, but on a single, simple, greenfield task (Peng et al. 2023). Context matters. METR’s 2026 follow-up could not produce a reliable estimate at all: too many developers declined to submit tasks they did not want to do without AI, which skewed the sample (METR 2026). That says more about adoption than productivity, but it says it loudly.
So hand-written code is a minority, not a rounding error. And the variable that decides what happens next is not adoption but trust, because trust decides whether a human still has to open the file.

title: The Last Programming Language Won’t Be for Humans
text:
3. Six futures on one map
Any proposal for the future of programming can be placed on two axes: who reads the code (humans, or only machines) and how it is represented (text tokens, or latent vectors). Hover over a point to see its trajectory, its evidence, and what would break it.



                        
                                            
Figure 1: Six scenarios for the future of programming. Everything in production sits bottom-left; every research trajectory pushes up and right.


The question that matters is what would move the industry along that diagonal, and whether every step on it is one we should want. Here are the six scenarios in brief.

S0 · Plateau: “AI as autocomplete”

Trajectory. Adoption without trust. Agents draft, humans review, and code stays multilingual and human-owned.
Evidence. The trust numbers and METR’s measured slowdown above (Stack Overflow 2025; Becker et al. 2025).
Breaks if. Trust and measured productivity rise together.
Status. Today. This is the null hypothesis, and the data currently supports it better than any alternative.



S1 · English on top: “The prompt is the program”

Trajectory. Karpathy’s arc: English in, code out, code never opened. Source becomes a build artifact.
Evidence. Agents alone write about 47% of professional developers’ code; Google reports 75% (JetBrains Research 2026; Semafor 2026).
Breaks if. Dijkstra’s precision objection bites. Already 45% of developers say debugging AI code takes longer than writing it (Stack Overflow 2025).
Status. In production, though “never opened” is aspirational: about half of developers still check every commit (Sonar 2026).



S2 · Typed bridge: “The spec is the source”

Trajectory. Languages that give agents machine-checkable feedback win. Humans read types, contracts and specifications; machines write the function bodies.
Evidence. TypeScript overtook Python as GitHub’s most-used language in 2025, a shift GitHub partly credits to AI (GitHub 2025). JavaScript/TypeScript and Go developers delegate 54–55% of their code to agents, against 33% for C and C++ (JetBrains Research 2026). Closed-loop pipelines such as Clover check generated Dafny code against its own annotations and docstrings (C. Sun et al. 2023).
Breaks if. Verification tooling stays niche while AI code passes security tests only 56% of the time (Veracode 2026).
Status. In production for types; pilot stage for proofs.



S3 · Compressed grammar: “Same meaning, fewer tokens”

Trajectory. Keep the language but strip out the parts only humans need. Humans see Python; the model sees a token-lean twin.
Evidence. Formatting alone is 13–15% of Java, C# and C++ tokens, and SimPy trims a further 10–13% with identical syntax trees (Pan et al. 2026; Z. Sun et al. 2024). Section 4 has the details.
Breaks if. Tokenizers disappear, or models stay clumsy in unfamiliar notation (Gate 3).
Status. Research prototype.



S4 · Universal IR: “One machine language”

Trajectory. An AI-native intermediate representation one rung above LLVM: the thing agents write and exchange, with English above it and machine code below.
Evidence. LLVM, MLIR and WebAssembly are already universal, unreadable targets, and the Platonic Representation Hypothesis suggests model internals are converging (Huh et al. 2024).
Breaks if. No cross-vendor standard emerges. Every lab has its own tokenizer and its own representation space.
Status. Analogy only. No artifact exists yet.



S5 · Neuralese: “No language”

Trajectory. Agents exchange activations, not text. Language is generated only when a human asks for it.
Evidence. DroidSpeak, Cache-to-Cache, Coconut, Gibberlink, and a decade of emergent-communication research (Liu et al. 2024; Fu et al. 2026; Hao et al. 2024; Starkov and Pidkuiko 2025; Lazaridou and Baroni 2020).
Breaks if. Monitorability requirements and regulation insist on a readable trace (Korbak et al. 2025).
Status. Lab.

title: The Last Programming Language Won’t Be for Humans
text:
4. What code costs a machine
Programming languages were designed for three audiences: the machine that runs the code, the person who writes it, and the person who reads it six months later. Language models are a fourth audience, and they pay for code in tokens.
Code is more predictable than prose. In 2012, Hindle and colleagues showed that source code has markedly lower cross-entropy than English under the same n-gram models: it is “natural” in the sense of being repetitive and conventional (Hindle et al. 2012). Casalnuovo, Sagae and Devanbu later confirmed the gap across corpora and model families (Casalnuovo, Sagae, and Devanbu 2019). Shannon had estimated printed English at roughly one bit per character (Shannon 1951). Delétang and colleagues tied that tradition to today’s models: a language model is a general-purpose compressor, and its loss is a compression rate (Delétang et al. 2024). Seen this way, any token the model could have predicted is overhead. It is there for some other reader.
A coding agent pays that overhead in two ways. The surface cost is the tokens needed to write the program down. The process cost is the tokens the agent burns reasoning, compiling, failing and revising on its way to a working program. The two are measured differently, and they rank languages differently.



                                                
Figure 2: Two bills for the same program. Left: output tokens a coding agent spends relative to Python on the same problems, after controlling for problem difficulty (Wu, Anderson and Guha 2026); faded bars are not statistically significant. Right: share of tokens that are whitespace, indentation and line breaks only (Pan et al. 2026).


Process cost. Wu, Anderson and Guha ran five current models as coding agents on the same 100 competitive-programming problems in Python, Java, Rust and OCaml: 2,000 runs in all (Wu, Anderson, and Guha 2026). A mixed-effects model let them compare languages on identical problems. Every model was cheapest in Python. OCaml cost 1.28–1.69× as many output tokens across all five. Rust (1.07–1.57×) and Java (0.85–1.34×) depended on the model, and Gemma was the one model where neither penalty was significant.
The mechanism is the interesting part. The extra tokens do not come from longer programs; they come from struggle. In Gemma’s stalled OCaml runs, 92% of the failed intermediate solutions were compile errors: the agent was fighting the syntax, not the algorithm. GPT-5.5 fell back to Python to prototype on 27% of OCaml problems before translating. The authors point to training data: The Stack v2 holds roughly 200 GB each of Python and Java, but only 12 GB of Rust and even less OCaml. They add their own caveat: these are self-contained problems, and repository-scale work may behave differently.
Surface cost. Martin Alderson ran the GPT-4 tokenizer over Rosetta Code solutions to the same tasks in 19 popular languages. He found a 2.6× spread, from Clojure (the most compact, at 109 tokens per task) to C (the most verbose). Dynamic languages generally won by skipping type declarations, with Haskell and F# close behind thanks to type inference. In a later run, J, an array language written in plain ASCII, averaged about 70 tokens. APL’s famous terseness, by contrast, did not survive tokenization: its unusual glyphs each split into several tokens (Alderson 2026). Surface cost depends on how well the tokenizer knows the notation, not just on how short the code looks.
The right-hand panel isolates the purest surface cost: formatting. On The Stack v2, whitespace, indentation and line breaks make up 14.7% of the tokens in Java and 13.2% in C# and C++, but only 4.0% in Python, where indentation carries meaning (Pan et al. 2026). Roughly one token in seven in a Java file exists only so that a human can read it. In the authors’ code-completion experiments, advanced models lost essentially nothing when the formatting was stripped out.
The next step is to redesign the grammar itself for the model. Sun and colleagues’ SimPy rewrites Python’s grammar to drop the tokens and layout only humans need, while keeping the abstract syntax tree identical, so programs convert losslessly in both directions. It cuts token usage by 13.5% for CodeLlama and 10.4% for GPT-4, with task performance maintained or improved (Z. Sun et al. 2024). Token Sugar extends the idea with reversible shorthands for recurring code patterns (Z. Sun et al. 2025). Humans see Python; the model sees something terser.
To see what the process-cost multipliers mean for a real bill, pick a model and a workload.

processCost = ({
  "Claude Sonnet 4.6": {Python: 1, Java: 1.18, Rust: 1.16, OCaml: 1.28},
  "GPT-5.5":           {Python: 1, Java: 1.30, Rust: 1.36, OCaml: 1.30},
  "GLM-5.2":           {Python: 1, Java: 1.34, Rust: 1.57, OCaml: 1.54},
  "Qwen 3.6":          {Python: 1, Java: 1.21, Rust: 1.20, OCaml: 1.69},
  "Gemma 4":           {Python: 1, Java: 0.85, Rust: 1.07, OCaml: 1.44}
})
viewof model = Inputs.select(Object.keys(processCost), {label: "Model", value: "GPT-5.5"})
viewof monthlyTokens = Inputs.range([1, 500], {
  value: 50, step: 1,
  label: "Output tokens per month if written in Python (millions)"
})
viewof price = Inputs.range([0.5, 30], {
  value: 10, step: 0.5,
  label: "Price per million output tokens (USD)"
})
costs = Object.entries(processCost[model]).map(([lang, m]) =>
  ({lang, m, cost: m * monthlyTokens * price}))
Plot.plot({
  marginLeft: 70,
  height: 260,
  x: {label: null, domain: ["Python", "Java", "Rust", "OCaml"]},
  y: {label: "USD per month", grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.barY(costs, {x: "lang", y: "cost", fill: "#534AB7"}),
    Plot.text(costs, {x: "lang", y: "cost",
      text: d => `$${Math.round(d.cost).toLocaleString()} (×${d.m.toFixed(2)})`, dy: -8}),
    Plot.ruleY([0])
  ]
})











































Readability, in other words, is a tax. It has always been worth paying, because humans read code. The rest of this post asks what happens to the tax when they stop.

title: The Last Programming Language Won’t Be for Humans
section: 5. Four gates between agents and neuralese
text:
5. Four gates between agents and neuralese
Here is the argument that started this post. Agents keep improving, so more people rely on them. Human supervision shifts from reading code to testing what it does. With no one reading it, code no longer needs to be readable, so the language is free to optimize for tokens. It converges on a single machine-facing representation. Eventually agents skip language altogether and exchange latent state directly.
Every arrow in that chain is a gate, and each gate has a metric you can watch.






flowchart LR
  S1["S1 English on top"] -->|"G1 agents ownthe debug loop"| S2["S2 Typed bridgespec is the source"]
  S2 -->|"G2 review movesto specs and tests"| G3{"G3 where is tokenpressure absorbed?"}
  G3 -->|"in the language"| S3["S3 Compressed grammar"]
  G3 -->|"in the model"| S4["S4 Universal IR"]
  S3 --> S4
  S4 -->|"G4 auditableprojection kept?"| S5["S5 Neuralese"]





Figure 3: The chain from coding agents to neuralese. Each arrow is a gate that current data either supports or contradicts.





Gate 1: agents must own the debug loop
“Test the outputs instead of reading the code” frees humans only if the agent also fixes what fails. The moment a person opens the file to debug, the pressure for readable code is back. So the thesis is really a claim about agent reliability, not about languages. Current data cuts against it: 45% of developers say debugging AI code takes longer than writing it (Stack Overflow 2025), and 96% do not fully trust it (Sonar 2026). METR sharpens the point. Roughly half of the test-passing SWE-bench Verified pull requests written by agents between mid-2024 and late 2025 would not have been merged by the repositories’ own maintainers (Whitfill et al. 2026). Passing the tests is not the same as being done.






Note



The share of developers who say debugging AI code takes longer than writing it, and the share of agent pull requests merged without human edits. Gate 1 opens when the first falls and the second rises.




Gate 2: tests are weaker than reading
Tests check what you thought to test. Security, privacy and side effects are exactly what you didn’t. Veracode tracked more than 100 models across four snapshots and found the security pass rate stuck at 56%. Syntax success was near 100%, yet nearly half of tasks introduced a vulnerability, with Python passing 63% of the time and Java only 30% (Veracode 2026). Veracode tests raw models with no security prompting or human review, so the figure measures how often flaws are generated, not how often they ship. But review is precisely the step this chain proposes to remove.
The remedy is specification and proof: the S2 world of Dafny, Lean and Clover. That means the human-facing language does not disappear; it moves up a level. Humans stop typing code, but they do not stop writing precise text.






Note



Adoption of verified-code tooling in CI pipelines, and the continued drift of language share toward statically typed languages.




Gate 3: the model may absorb the token pressure, not the language
Grammar redesign saves 10–13% of tokens; stripping formatting saves 4–15%. Meanwhile, the price of a given level of capability has been falling by roughly an order of magnitude a year (Appenzeller 2024), and tokenizer-free architectures have arrived. Meta’s Byte Latent Transformer reads raw bytes, grouped into patches by how predictable the next byte is, with no tokenizer at all, and matches token-based models at the 8-billion-parameter scale (Pagnoni et al. 2024). If that approach wins, the inefficiency S3 targets vanishes inside the model, with no change to the language.
Section 4’s process-cost data adds a second objection. Agents are cheapest in the languages they have seen most, and burn tokens fighting the syntax of the ones they have seen least. A brand-new, token-optimal language would begin life as the least familiar language in the world (OCaml’s problem, magnified) until models were trained on it at scale.
So “less supervision leads to token pressure” holds, but “token pressure leads to a new language” is the weakest link in the chain. The likelier outcome is that the language stays, the tokenizer dies, and S3 is skipped.






Note



Whether a frontier lab ships a tokenizer-free production model, and whether any vendor ships an AI-oriented grammar. Either would settle the question.




Gate 4: neuralese needs permission, not just capability
The chain needs less human oversight; governance is moving the other way. Korbak and colleagues, writing across the major labs, argue that the ability to monitor a model’s chain of thought is a safety property worth protecting in how models are built (Korbak et al. 2025). Liability and regulation both push toward a readable trace. The technology is not ready either. Cache-to-Cache works across models only through a learned projector between specific pairs (Fu et al. 2026), and cross-vendor latent communication would need a standard nobody has agreed on. The nearest precedent is the Model Context Protocol, which went from announcement to de facto standard for tool calls in about a year (Anthropic 2024). S5 will most likely arrive as a capability permitted only where S4 keeps an auditable projection alongside it.






Note



Any cross-vendor cache or latent-state protocol, and whether monitorability requirements make it into regulation.


Put the gates back into the chain and the argument changes shape. Agents become reliable enough to own the debug loop (Gate 1). Human review moves to specs and tests (Gate 2, S2). Code stops being written for human eyes. Efficiency pressure appears, but tokenizer-free models absorb it instead of new grammars (Gate 3, skipping S3). Multi-agent systems adopt latent communication wherever auditability survives (Gate 4, S4 and S5). The destination looks similar; the route does not.

title: The Last Programming Language Won’t Be for Humans
text:
6. What “universal” actually means
The universal language already exists; it just isn’t one anybody writes. LLVM IR (LLVM Project, n.d.b), MLIR (LLVM Project, n.d.a) and WebAssembly (WebAssembly Community Group, n.d.) are universal, machine-targeted and effectively unreadable. Dozens of source languages compile into them, and nobody complains that they cannot read the result. My prediction is an AI-native IR one rung above LLVM: the thing agents write and exchange, with English above it and machine code below.
Three lines of research suggest this is more than an analogy.
The representations are converging. The Platonic Representation Hypothesis holds that, as models scale, their internal representations converge across architectures and modalities toward a shared statistical model of reality (Huh et al. 2024). If internal representations converge, a shared external one becomes an engineering problem.
The artifacts exist. DroidSpeak passes embedding and key-value caches between agents built on the same base model instead of re-tokenizing text, cutting prefill latency by up to 2.78× with negligible loss of accuracy (Liu et al. 2024). Cache-to-Cache extends this across different models using a learned projector and a neural cache fuser (Fu et al. 2026). Coconut does the same thing within a single model, reasoning in continuous latent space instead of decoding tokens (Hao et al. 2024).
The precedent is old. In 2017, Lewis and colleagues’ negotiation agents drifted from English into a shorthand of their own once the reward stopped caring about English (Lewis et al. 2017). Lazaridou and Baroni survey a decade of research in which agents invent communication protocols under pressure (Lazaridou and Baroni 2020). And in 2025, the Gibberlink hackathon demo showed two voice agents switching from English to a data-over-sound protocol once they recognized each other. It was scripted by prompt rather than emergent, but it went viral because it made the idea concrete (Starkov and Pidkuiko 2025). The S5 future has already happened in the lab, more than once.
So the universal coding language is real. It is an IR, it sits below humans, and it will probably take two forms: a symbolic one for auditing and a latent one for speed.

title: The Last Programming Language Won’t Be for Humans
section: 7. Not a winner, but a stack
text:
7. Not a winner, but a stack
Put the scenarios together and they stop looking like competitors. They are layers.






flowchart TB
  H["Humans · intent in English (S1)"] --> P["Spec · types, contracts, proofs (S2)the human-readable contract"]
  P --> I["Universal IR · machine-facing, token-optimal (S4)"]
  I --> N["Neuralese · latent exchange between agents (S5)"]
  N -.->|"auditable projection"| P





Figure 4: The likely endpoint is a stack, not a winner. The compiler stack never deleted a rung either.




Assembly still runs under C, which still runs under Python. The likeliest endpoint is S1 as the human interface, S2 as the verifiable contract, and S4 and S5 as the machine representation, with S3 a transitional hack that tokenizer-free models make unnecessary.
Three signals will tell you which scenario is winning:

The trust number. If the share of developers who trust AI output climbs back past 40% in Stack Overflow’s survey while “debugging takes longer” falls, Gate 1 is opening.
Verified-code adoption. If proof-carrying or contract-checked generation moves from research into CI pipelines, Gate 2 is holding the human-facing layer at the spec.
A cross-vendor latent protocol. The first standard that lets one lab’s agent hand its cache to another’s, with an auditable projection, is the moment S4 and S5 leave the lab.

Until then, the honest reading of the data is S0 sliding into S1. That is a long way from coding being dead. It is the distance between “nobody types assembly” and “assembly is dead.”
Hands will leave the keyboard. What they leave behind is the spec: the one artifact that has to be precise, checkable, and readable by the people who bear the consequences. The spec is the new source code.

title: MAE vs JEPA: Two Ways to Learn Representations Without Labels
text: I am using this post as a working note while learning self-supervised learning for tactile sensing. The two families I keep comparing are Masked Autoencoders (MAE) and Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPA).

title: MAE vs JEPA: Two Ways to Learn Representations Without Labels
text:
The shared goal
Both methods try to learn useful representations without requiring manual labels. Instead of asking a model to predict a human-provided class, we create a prediction problem from the data itself.
For tactile sensing, this is appealing because labeled tactile data can be expensive. But the robot can collect lots of interaction data: normal forces, shear forces, contact patches, and temporal sequences.

title: MAE vs JEPA: Two Ways to Learn Representations Without Labels
text:
MAE intuition
A Masked Autoencoder hides part of the input and trains the model to reconstruct what was removed. In vision, that means masking image patches. In tactile sensing, a similar idea could mask spatial taxels, temporal spans, or force channels.
The reconstruction target keeps the training signal concrete: the model must recover missing data.

title: MAE vs JEPA: Two Ways to Learn Representations Without Labels
text:
JEPA intuition
JEPA also predicts missing information, but it predicts in representation space rather than directly reconstructing pixels or sensor values. The model learns an embedding of visible context and predicts the embedding of the target.
This can encourage more semantic or task-useful representations because the model is not forced to reproduce every low-level detail.

title: MAE vs JEPA: Two Ways to Learn Representations Without Labels
text:
The question I care about
For tactile sensing, the right representation should preserve object-relevant properties: shape, contact distribution, slip, force direction, and possibly object count. I want to understand whether direct reconstruction or representation-space prediction gives better features for downstream inference.

title: MAE vs JEPA: Two Ways to Learn Representations Without Labels
text:
Open notes

What should be masked: time, taxels, force channels, or spatial regions?
Should shear and normal channels be treated symmetrically?
How much of the tactile signal is useful low-level detail versus nuisance variation?
Which downstream probe best reveals representation quality?

title: Simulating a Tactile Sensor in MuJoCo
text: One part of my UCL visit is about replicating a 3-channel tactile sensor in MuJoCo for data collection and training. The goal is not to build a perfect copy of the real sensor. The goal is to create a simulation that produces useful tactile structure for learning.

title: Simulating a Tactile Sensor in MuJoCo
text:
What needs to be simulated
A useful tactile simulation needs at least:

Contact location across the sensor surface.
Normal force at contact points.
Shear forces in two lateral directions.
Temporal changes as objects move, slip, or press into the surface.

The difficult part is matching the signal statistics closely enough that models trained on simulation learn transferable structure.

title: Simulating a Tactile Sensor in MuJoCo
text:
The modeling tradeoff
A high-fidelity tactile simulation can become expensive quickly. But a very simple proxy may miss the contact cues needed for downstream tasks. The practical question is where the approximation should live.
For representation learning, it may be enough for the simulation to capture the relationships between contact, shape, and force dynamics, even if every taxel is not physically perfect.

title: Simulating a Tactile Sensor in MuJoCo
text:
Data collection loop
The imagined loop is:

Sample objects, poses, and interactions in simulation.
Record normal and shear force maps over time.
Train MAE/JEPA-style models on the generated tactile streams.
Test whether the learned representation transfers to real tactile data.

title: Simulating a Tactile Sensor in MuJoCo
text:
Open questions

Which contact model best matches the real sensor behavior?
How much domain randomization is useful?
Should the network see raw forces or preprocessed tactile maps?
What downstream task best measures whether the simulation is good enough?

title: Normal and Shear Forces in Tactile Sensing
text: Touch is not just pressure. A tactile sensor can measure how hard an object presses into the surface, but also how contact moves sideways. That sideways information is often the clue that an object is slipping, rotating, or changing contact state.

title: Normal and Shear Forces in Tactile Sensing
text:
Three channels
The tactile setup I am learning from uses three force channels:

Normal force: how strongly the object presses into the sensor.
Shear-x: lateral force along one sensor axis.
Shear-y: lateral force along the other sensor axis.

Together, these channels describe richer contact mechanics than normal force alone.

title: Normal and Shear Forces in Tactile Sensing
text:
Why shear matters
If the normal force stays similar but shear changes, the object may be sliding or rotating. For in-hand manipulation, that can reveal object pose changes before the object visually moves in an obvious way.
This is especially relevant for shape and quantity inference. A pile of objects, a single larger object, and an object contacting at a different angle can produce different shear patterns even when the normal force magnitude is comparable.

title: Normal and Shear Forces in Tactile Sensing
text:
What I want from representations
The representation should make contact events legible. It should capture where contact occurs, how force flows across the sensor, and how those patterns evolve over time.
That is why tactile sensing is a good fit for self-supervised learning: the raw signal is rich, but the useful abstractions are not always obvious in advance.

title: Variational Quantum Eigensolver From Scratch
text:
VQE stands for Variational Quantum Eigensolver. It is a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm for estimating the lowest-energy eigenstate, or ground state, of a Hamiltonian.
This is a migrated and lightly cleaned version of my original Medium post.
Original post: https://medium.com/analytics-vidhya/variational-quantum-eigensolver-from-scratch-finding-ground-state-energy-of-hamiltonian-a5c13d5268f1

title: Variational Quantum Eigensolver From Scratch
text:
Variational Principle
If we have a Hamiltonian H with eigenstates and associated eigenvalues, then:
H |psi> = lambda |psi>
Here lambda is the energy for the state |psi>. For many possible states there are different energies, but one state has the smallest energy. That state is the ground state of the system. VQE gives us a practical way to search for that ground state.
The algorithm can be summarized in three parts:

Decomposition.
Circuit construction, including the ansatz and measurement basis.
Measurement and classical optimization.

title: Variational Quantum Eigensolver From Scratch
text:
Part 1: Decomposition
The first step is decomposing a Hamiltonian into Pauli matrices. Pauli matrices form a basis for the real vector space of 2 x 2 Hermitian matrices. That means any 2 x 2 Hermitian matrix can be written as a unique linear combination of Pauli matrices with real coefficients.
For a two-qubit Hamiltonian, we work with 4 x 4 Hermitian matrices and tensor products of Pauli terms. These terms tell us which basis to measure in, and their coefficients tell us how much weight each expectation value should receive in the final energy estimate.
For example, a decomposed two-qubit Hamiltonian may include terms such as:

I tensor I
X tensor X
Y tensor Y
Z tensor Z

Each term receives a coefficient from the decomposition.

title: Variational Quantum Eigensolver From Scratch
text:
Part 2: Circuit
Once the Hamiltonian is decomposed, we create circuits for the terms in the decomposition. The circuit has two central pieces.

Ansatz
The ansatz is a parameterized circuit that prepares the trial quantum state. In a VQE loop, the classical optimizer changes the ansatz parameters and the quantum circuit estimates the corresponding energy.
In the original experiment, the ansatz was chosen by trial and error. Different ansatz choices can produce similar performance, but the ansatz controls the set of states the algorithm can search.


Measurement basis
Quantum computers measure in the computational, or Z, basis by default. If we need expectation values in another basis, we rotate the state before measurement.
For a Hamiltonian with terms like:

I tensor I
X tensor X
Y tensor Y
Z tensor Z

the identity term does not need a circuit. The X tensor X term can be measured by rotating both qubits into the X basis. The Y tensor Y term can be measured by rotating both qubits into the Y basis. The Z tensor Z term can be measured directly after preparing the ansatz.

title: Variational Quantum Eigensolver From Scratch
text:
Part 3: Measurement
For each circuit, we measure probabilities for outcomes such as |00>, |01>, |10>, and |11>.
For a single qubit, measuring |0> corresponds to eigenvalue +1, and measuring |1> corresponds to eigenvalue -1. For two qubits, the sign for a measurement is the product of the two eigenvalues. For example, |01> gives:
(+1) x (-1) = -1
The expectation value is computed as:
sum(sign * probability)
After computing the expectation value for each circuit, we multiply by the corresponding Hamiltonian coefficient and add the terms together. That gives the current energy estimate.

title: Variational Quantum Eigensolver From Scratch
text:
VQE Algorithm
The VQE loop is:

Pick ansatz parameters.
Prepare the ansatz state on the quantum circuit.
Measure each Hamiltonian term in the correct basis.
Estimate the energy from expectation values.
Use a classical optimizer to update the ansatz parameters.
Repeat until the energy stops improving.

In the example from the original post, the lowest eigenvalue found was -1, corresponding to the ground-state estimate for the chosen Hamiltonian.

title: Variational Quantum Eigensolver From Scratch
text:
End Note
The most important thing I learned from coding VQE from scratch is that the quantum and classical pieces are tightly coupled. The quantum circuit gives noisy energy estimates; the classical optimizer decides where to search next. The ansatz sits between them and determines which states are reachable.

title: Variational Quantum Eigensolver From Scratch
text:
Why VQE is interesting
VQE is designed for near-term quantum computers because it keeps the quantum circuit relatively shallow and uses a classical optimizer for the outer loop. That makes it a useful algorithm to study when learning hybrid quantum-classical machine learning.

title: Linear Control on a Nonlinear Soft Surface
text:
Soft robotic systems are nonlinear almost by definition: fabrics deform, objects slide and roll, friction changes, and contact geometry matters. It is tempting to assume the controller must also be complex.
Our CASE 2025 paper explores a more pragmatic question: how far can a simple linear controller go on a nonlinear soft manipulation surface?

title: Linear Control on a Nonlinear Soft Surface
section: Why simple control is worth testing
text:
Why simple control is worth testing
Simple controllers are easier to tune, debug, and deploy. When hardware is new, a controller that reveals the important system behavior can be more useful than an opaque controller that only works in a narrow setup.
The goal was not to claim that the surface is linear. It was to test whether a linear controller can still produce useful manipulation when the actuation and object response are nonlinear.

title: Linear Control on a Nonlinear Soft Surface
text:
The manipulation loop
At a high level, the controller compares the current object position with the target, maps the error into actuator commands, and updates the surface shape. The soft surface then converts those changes into object motion.
The interesting part is that the controller can remain relatively simple while the physical surface performs much of the transformation.

title: Linear Control on a Nonlinear Soft Surface
text:
Takeaway
For grasp-free manipulation, the controller and hardware should be designed together. The surface is not just a passive floor; it is part of the computation.
Paper: DOI

title: Soft Manipulation With Fewer Actuators
text:
A common way to build a manipulation surface is to place many actuators under it. That can work, but it makes the platform expensive, mechanically dense, and difficult to scale.
In our RoboSoft 2025 paper, we explored a different design: a soft surface actuated by fewer vertical actuators, spaced far enough apart that the object can be much smaller than the distance between actuators. This creates a control problem because the surface is nonlinear and continuous, but it also creates a hardware opportunity: fewer actuators can cover a larger area.

title: Soft Manipulation With Fewer Actuators
text:
What the surface does
The surface changes shape, and the object moves because gravity, contact geometry, and surface deformation combine into a controllable motion field. The robot does not grasp the object. It changes the world under the object.

title: Soft Manipulation With Fewer Actuators
text:
Why heterogeneous objects matter
Real applications rarely contain one perfect object. Objects differ in weight, shape, size, fragility, and friction. A manipulation surface should not need a new gripper for every case.
That is why this line of work focuses on heterogeneous objects. The long-term question is whether a single soft surface can provide enough controllability while staying mechanically simple.

title: Soft Manipulation With Fewer Actuators
text:
What I learned
Hardware simplicity moves complexity into modeling, sensing, and control. That tradeoff is not automatically good, but it is interesting: if the surface can be controlled robustly, sparse actuation makes the system much easier to scale.
Paper: DOI

title: Scalable Surface-Based Manipulation Through Modularity
text: Robotic Manipulation Surfaces (RMS) move objects by deforming the surface they rest on. This makes them attractive for fragile, irregular, or food-like objects, where grasping can damage the item or require a specialized gripper. The difficulty is scale: dense actuator arrays can give fine control, but they become expensive and mechanically complex when the workspace grows.

title: Scalable Surface-Based Manipulation Through Modularity
text:
The core idea
The paper asks whether a manipulation surface can be made modular. Instead of building one very dense surface, we connect fabric-based modules and coordinate object movement across module boundaries. Adjacent modules share edge actuators, reducing actuator count from 4n^2 to (n + 1)^2 for an n x n grid.
In a 2 x 2 prototype, this gives a 1 x 1 m workspace with only 9 actuators.

title: Scalable Surface-Based Manipulation Through Modularity
text:
What makes it hard
Sharing actuators is efficient, but it mechanically couples neighboring modules. Moving one module can disturb objects on another module. The platform therefore needs both high-level path planning and low-level compensation.
Our framework combines:

Manhattan-style conflict-free path planning.
Directional object passing between modules.
A geometric PID controller for positioning.
Compensation strategies for passive-object disturbance.

title: Scalable Surface-Based Manipulation Through Modularity
text:
Result
The system achieves coordinated inter-module transfer and sub-centimeter positioning for heterogeneous objects, including fragile items. Compensation reduced passive-object displacement by 59-78% across the measured configurations.

title: Scalable Surface-Based Manipulation Through Modularity
text:
Why I care about this
For me, the interesting part is not only that a surface can move objects. It is that manipulation can be treated as a property of a distributed surface: hardware design, geometry, and control all contribute. That feels like a promising route toward scalable manipulation in logistics, food processing, and other settings where objects are too varied for one gripper.
Paper: arXiv:2601.21884

title: Getting Started With Webots
text: Webots is a simulation software package for rapidly prototyping mobile robots and autonomous systems. It provides a 3D physics-based environment with support for sensors, controllers, data visualization, and robot models.

title: Getting Started With Webots
section: What can Webots be used for?
text:
What can Webots be used for?

Mobile robot prototyping for academic research and industry.
Robot locomotion research, including legged robots.
Multi-agent and swarm robotics.
Adaptive behavior experiments such as genetic algorithms.
Teaching robotics and running robot contests.

title: Getting Started With Webots
text:
What you should know first
You can use Webots with C, C++, Java, Python, or MATLAB. If you want to create custom robot models or environments, it also helps to know some 3D graphics concepts and the VRML97 descriptive language.
A Webots simulation typically includes:

A world file (.wbt) that defines robots and the environment.
Controller programs that run the robot logic.
Optional physics plugins for custom physics behavior.

title: Getting Started With Webots
text:
Create the first project
Open Webots and go to Wizards > New Project Directory. Name the project bug, name the world file bug.wbt, and select the options to add a rectangular arena.
Before adding a robot, change the arena size from 1 x 1 m to 2 x 2 m by editing RectangleArena > floorSize.

title: Getting Started With Webots
text:
Add an e-puck robot
Click Add in the scene tree, then choose PROTO nodes > robots > gctronic > e-puck > E-puck. The robot should appear in the arena. Save the world before running the simulation.
The e-puck has a default obstacle avoidance controller, so you can run the simulation immediately to see the robot move.

time_step = 32

right_motor = robot.getMotor("right wheel motor")

right_motor.setVelocity(0.0)

    right_speed = max_speed * 0.25

    right_motor.setVelocity(right_speed)

title: HMM-Based POS Tagger on the Brown Corpus
text:
Write a program in Python to implement an HMM-based part-of-speech (POS) tagger for English.
Dataset: the Brown corpus (via NLTK), which contains words paired with their POS tags.
Code: https://github.com/pratik-ingle/HMM-tagger

title: HMM-Based POS Tagger on the Brown Corpus
text:
Mathematical model
An HMM tagger is a special case of Bayesian inference. We model \(P(Y \mid X)\), the probability of a tag sequence given a word sequence, using two kinds of probabilities:

Emission probability: the likelihood of a word \(w_i\) given a tag \(t_i\), \(P(w_i \mid t_i)\).
Transition probability: the likelihood of a tag given the previous tags, \(P(t_i \mid t_{i-1}, t_{i-2}, \dots, t_{i-k})\).

The best tag sequence is
\[
\hat{T} = \arg\max_T \prod_i P(w_i \mid t_i)\, P(t_i \mid t_{i-1}).
\]

Training
Both probabilities are estimated from counts in the training set:
\[
P(t_i \mid t_{i-1}) = \frac{C(t_{i-1}, t_i)}{C(t_{i-1})}, \qquad
P(w_i \mid t_i) = \frac{C(t_i, w_i)}{C(t_i)}.
\]


Viterbi algorithm
\[
V_t(j) = \max_i V_{t-1}(i)\, a_{ij}\, b_j(o_t)
\]
where \(V_{t-1}(i)\) is the previous Viterbi path probability, \(a_{ij}\) the transition probability, and \(b_j(o_t)\) the state observation (emission) likelihood.
The total number of possible tag sequences is \(T^W\) for \(T\) tags and \(W\) words, which is why dynamic programming is needed.


Assumptions

The probability of a word depends only on its POS tag, and is independent of other words and tags.
The probability of a tag depends only on the previous tag (bigram assumption).

title: HMM-Based POS Tagger on the Brown Corpus
text:
Procedure


1. Split the corpus
Insert start <s> and end <\s> symbols in each sentence, then hold out the first 10 sentences for testing.
from nltk.corpus import brown

p = brown.tagged_sents()
brown_corpus = []
for i in p:
    i.insert(0, ('<s>', '<s>'))
    i.insert(len(i), ('<\\s>', '<\\s>'))
    brown_corpus.append(i)

brown_test = []
brown_train = []
sen = 0
for i in brown_corpus:
    sen += 1
    if sen <= 10:
        brown_test.append(i)
    else:
        brown_train.append(i)


2. Count patterns in the training set
We need three frequency tables:

fre_wordtag: frequency of each (word, tag) pair
fre_tag: frequency of each tag
fre_bi_tag: frequency of each tag given its previous tag

from collections import Counter

def fre(x):
    types = Counter(tuple(item) for item in x)
    freq = list(types.items())
    freq.sort(key=lambda f: f[1], reverse=True)
    return freq

# flatten training sentences into (word, tag) pairs
brown_words_tag = [j for i in brown_train for j in i]
fre_wordtag = fre(brown_words_tag)

# tag frequencies
brown_tag = [j[1] for i in brown_train for j in i]
fre_tag = list(Counter(brown_tag).items())
fre_tag.sort(key=lambda f: f[1], reverse=True)


3. Turn counts into probabilities
Emission probabilities \(P(w_i \mid t_i) = C(t_i, w_i) / C(t_i)\):
probWiti = []
for i in fre_wordtag:
    for j in fre_tag:
        if i[0][1] == j[0]:
            probWiti.append([i[0], i[1] / j[1]])
Transition probabilities \(P(t_i \mid t_{i-1}) = C(t_{i-1}, t_i) / C(t_{i-1})\), built from tag bigrams (skipping the <\s> → <s> sentence boundary):
bi_tag = []
x = len(brown_words_tag)
for j in range(x - 1):
    temp = [brown_words_tag[j][1], brown_words_tag[j + 1][1]]
    if temp != ['<\\s>', '<s>']:
        bi_tag.append(temp)

fre_bi_tag = fre(bi_tag)

probbitag = []
for i in fre_bi_tag:
    for j in fre_tag:
        if i[0][0] == j[0]:
            probbitag.append([i[0], i[1] / j[1]])
The set of all tags seen in training is simply:
pos_tag = [i[0] for i in fre_tag]
Because a word’s probability depends on its tag and a tag’s probability depends on the previous tag, there is no UNK tag in the tagger itself; unknown words are handled separately below.


4. Viterbi decoding
With the probabilities in hand we build, for one test sentence, an emission lattice (only entries with non-zero emission probability, since a zero would zero out the whole path) and the set of transition probabilities among the tags that sentence can take.
sentance = brown_test[4]   # pick any of the first 10 test sentences
l = len(sentance)

lattic_emission = [[] for _ in range(l)]
sen_tag = []
for i in range(l):
    for j in probWiti:
        if sentance[i][0] == j[0][0]:
            lattic_emission[i].append(j)
            if j[0][1] not in sen_tag:
                sen_tag.append(j[0][1])
    if len(lattic_emission[i]) == 0:
        # unknown word: treat as 'NN' with probability 0.11
        lattic_emission[i].append([(sentance[i][0], 'NN'), 0.11])

# transition probabilities restricted to tags that appear in this sentence
tran_tag = [(i, j) for i in sen_tag for j in sen_tag]
tran_pro = [j for i in tran_tag for j in probbitag if i == j[0]]

# keep the highest-emission tag for each word, then chain transitions
max_emission = []
sequence = []
for i in lattic_emission:
    i.sort(key=lambda e: e[1], reverse=True)
    max_emission.append(i)

vi = []
for i in range(len(max_emission) - 1):
    vi.append((max_emission[i][0][0][1], max_emission[i + 1][0][0][1]))
    sequence.append(max_emission[i][0][0])
sequence.append(('<\\s>', '<\\s>'))

Vj = []
for i in range(len(vi)):
    for j in tran_pro:
        if vi[i] == j[0]:
            Vj.append(max_emission[i][0][1] * j[1])

def viterbi(Vj):
    result = 1
    for x in Vj:
        result *= x
    return result

print(sequence, '\n', viterbi(Vj))


5. Accuracy
count = 0
for i in range(len(sentance)):
    if sentance[i] == sequence[i]:
        count += 1
accuracy = count / len(sentance) * 100
print("accuracy of HMM tagger for given sentence is", accuracy)

Viterbi returns the most probable tag sequence with a sentence probability of about \(5 \times 10^{-33}\). Compared against the gold tags, accuracy on this sentence is only 53.8%, lower than the unigram and bigram taggers from earlier assignments. Two reasons: the Brown tagset is very fine-grained (phrase-level suffixes such as -HL, -TL, -NC split what would otherwise be one tag), and the corpus is case sensitive, so the same word gets different tags depending on capitalisation. The HMM does, however, do a better job at identifying phrases.

title: HMM-Based POS Tagger on the Brown Corpus
text:
Unknown words
Words not seen in training are tagged NN, since most training words are nouns. In earlier assignments tagging everything as NN gave about 11% accuracy, so unknown words are given an emission probability of 0.11 in the Viterbi product.

title: HMM-Based POS Tagger on the Brown Corpus
text:
Comparison with other taggers
Exhaustive HMM decoding is expensive: with \(n\) tags and \(m\) words there are \(n^m\) tag sequences, which is why the Viterbi dynamic-programming algorithm is used to find the optimal one.
Like other stochastic taggers, an HMM tagger finds the most likely tag for a word or sequence of words. Unlike greedy taggers that tag one word at a time, the HMM tags a whole sentence at once, choosing the sequence that maximises
P(word | tag) * P(tag | previous n tags)
The HMM outperforms the simpler taggers here, but it is not the most accurate option: an interpolated tagger can do better.

title: HMM-Based POS Tagger on the Brown Corpus
text:
HMM and ambiguity
Because the HMM considers the whole sentence, it can surface ambiguity: an ambiguous sentence gets different probabilities for its different tag sequences, and the most plausible reading is the one with the highest probability.

title: HMM-Based POS Tagger on the Brown Corpus

Extend the transition model to depend on three or more previous tags (trigram or higher-order HMM).
Replace the count-based model with a neural sequence tagger.

title: Research
text:
Current Directions

Soft manipulation surfaces
Robotic manipulation surfaces deform underneath an object and move it by changing contact geometry. The central challenge is balancing three goals that often fight each other: precise control, hardware simplicity, and scalable workspace size.
My PhD work explores fabric-based surfaces actuated by sparse, coordinated vertical actuators. Instead of treating manipulation as a grasping problem, I model how surface deformation can create usable object motion for positioning, transfer, and handling heterogeneous objects.


Modular grasp-free manipulation
A single soft surface is useful, but many applications need larger workspaces. Modular surfaces can expand the workspace, but transferring objects across module boundaries is difficult because neighboring modules mechanically interact through the surface.
My recent work studies shared-boundary actuation, hierarchical planning, directional object passing, and compensation for passive-object disturbance caused by mechanically coupled modules.


Tactile sensing and self-supervised learning
During my UCL visit, I have been working on tactile sensing for in-hand object shape and quantity inference with a leapXela-style tactile robot setup. The project involves self-supervised representation learning with Masked Autoencoders (MAE) and Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPA), plus MuJoCo simulation of normal and shear tactile channels for data collection.


Earlier work: swarm robotics and collectives
Before my PhD, I worked on collective robotics and decision-making in dynamic environments. This included multi-robot foraging, moving depots, collective decision models, and quantum-inspired approaches to identifying influential agents in swarms.
